schema_note: Entry fields: text, form (nb/nn/en), subject (person/animal/org), difficulty, note, genres (genre ids the clause is plausible in; [] = never sampled), and optional constraints on the record's subject: gender (M/F), age_range [min,max], origin (native/foreign), nationalities (list of nationality adjectives the subject must have), status (employed/unemployed/retired/uforetrygd), partner (opposite: implies an opposite-sex partner), marital (the MARITAL_STATUS value the clause implies). Negatives (version 4; version 5 adds the `nearmiss_v5` batch): `plantable` marks near-miss texts that are null under every type, so a benchmark run may plant them verbatim and leave them unlabelled; `genres` restricts them like a clause, `gender` (M/F) restricts the subject, and `also_labelled` maps a TYPE to a substring of the text that is a real value of that other type and is labelled as such (the near-miss is only for the type the negative is filed under). Negatives may carry `age_range` like a clause; without one a negative is for adult subjects only. `as_type` relabels an entry as another type when sampled (a civil-status clause with no kinship noun filed under FAMILY_RELATION is MARITAL_STATUS). Version 5: a negative's `text` may hold `{PRON}` (han/hun, han/ho), `{POSS}` (hans/hennes, hans/hennar) and `{OBJ}` (ham/henne, han/henne), filled from the document subject's gender and the document's form when the negative is planted; the planted text, and what G2 searches for, is the filled one. A near-miss that needs a subject carries its own (`og {PRON} svarte ...`) and starts with a coordinating word so it cannot open a sentence and be capitalised. `why_not` begins with the ANNOTATION_SPEC rule that makes the text a null; `kind` is one of refusal (B7), absence (B15), generic, ordinary, third_party, institution, id_shaped (B20), lawful, physical; `origin` names the batch so `gendoc_dataset.py extend-negatives` can partition it without moving earlier entries. Version 6 (`origin: multi_v6`) adds the entries several instances of one type are drawn from, and these optional fields on the multi-instance types (CRIMINAL, HEALTH, MEDICATION, BEHAVIORAL_PATTERN, FINANCIAL, ECONOMIC_STATUS, FAMILY_RELATION): `topic` (what the clause is about; no two clauses of one type in one document share a topic), `also` (further topics an entry occupies, e.g. a threat clause that mentions a weapon), `group` (at most one topic of a group per document across all types: one psychiatric condition, one general financial condition, one infection, the partner and the children of FAMILY_RELATION), `polarity` (poor or rich, which the means a clause implies; one per document across FINANCIAL and ECONOMIC_STATUS), and for FINANCIAL `kind` (debt, headline, asset, income, unspecified) with a numeric `amount` in NOK, so that the debts listed beside a headline total never exceed it. `subject: animal` entries are drawn only by the genres that list the type in `animal_types` (a veterinary record's HEALTH findings). Genre ids added for particular kinds of document: `crime` (police, prosecution, court, restraining-order, forensics and clearance documents), `forensics`, `bank`, `debt` (debt counselling, inkasso, bank AML), `barnevern`, `school` and, for the veterinary documents, `vet_clinical` and `vet_inspection`; a genre draws them through `clause_genres`.
